extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, and research-funding policymakers studying gender bias and fairness in grant peer review
extracted.subtask_short: reanalyzing gender bias in grant review
extracted.subtask_description: Reanalysis of Wennerås & Wold's 1997 study to assess gender and nepotism effects in peer review scores and in subsequent grant allocation, using field-normalized performance metrics and panel-standardized review scores. Focus is on statistical modelling and panel-level outcomes to evaluate whether biased review scores translate into biased funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence scores (reviewer-assessed competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer-assigned 'competence' score for applicants (as used by W&W), which can differ systematically by gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper finds gender bias in competence scores but a smaller 'male bonus' than originally reported; competence scores should be analyzed after field-normalizing performance and panel-standardizing review scores to separate performance effects from reviewer bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male bonus
rubrics_metrics.description: The extra measured advantage male applicants appear to receive in review scores (Wennerås & Wold reported a 'male bonus' equal to three Science papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify male bonus in comparable units (e.g., equivalent number of high-impact papers). The reanalysis found a male bonus about one-fifth of W&W's original estimate, indicating sensitivity to normalization and modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer affiliation (nepotism) bonus
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed score advantage for applicants who share affiliation or close links with reviewers (labelled 'reviewer affiliation (or nepotism) bonus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report the nepotism bonus separately from gender effects; field-normalization and panel-standardization reduce such effects and show a smaller nepotism bonus than originally reported by W&W.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation letter bonus
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed positive effect on scores linked to the presence or content of recommendation/support letters (the 'recommendation letter bonus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate this bonus while controlling for performance indicators; the reanalysis reports a reduced magnitude compared to the original study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalizing performance scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust applicants' performance indicators by scientific field before analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-normalization is required to make publication and citation measures comparable across fields and avoid confounding when estimating gender/nepotism effects; the authors explicitly 'field-normaliz[e] the performance scores' prior to assessing reviewer bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-standardizing review scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize reviewer scores across different panels to remove panel-specific scaling differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel-standardization helps control for between-panel differences in scoring leniency/strictness; the authors 'panel-standardiz[e] the review scores' to better compare scores and estimate bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate analysis of panel scores and grant allocation decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between bias in panel review scores and bias in the final grant decisions (allocation outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume biased panel scores will automatically lead to biased funding: analyze grant decisions directly and also at the panel level, since aggregated panel-score bias may not translate into allocation bias except in specific panels (the paper finds allocation bias in two panels only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-level analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate outcomes and biases at the level of individual evaluation panels rather than only in aggregated data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study emphasizes panel-level investigation because two panels where grant-decision bias was found accounted for a substantial share of female applicants; results can vary widely across panels and may be masked by aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generalized linear models and regression reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ GLMs (linear and logistic models) to estimate associations and report model fit (e.g., pseudo R^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used SPSS27 and GLMs; because GLMs do not provide R^2 by default, they also ran linear and logistic regressions to obtain (pseudo) R^2 values. Report modeling choices, diagnostics and goodness-of-fit to support conclusions about bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for applicant age / birth year
rubrics_metrics.description: Include age (or year of birth) as a covariate because age is associated with grant and career success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes age effects in prior work (younger better in some contexts) and includes age controls where relevant; ignoring age can confound gender effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bibliometric indicators (publication counts and journal impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure applicant performance using publication counts and indicators of impact (e.g., publications in Science/Nature, citation-based measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use field-normalized bibliometric indicators and multiple measures to better capture performance; equate effect sizes to intuitive units (e.g., 'equivalent Science papers') where helpful but beware of overinterpreting single high-impact counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for productivity/performance when assessing bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for measurable research performance so that observed score differences can be separated into performance vs bias components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reanalysis includes performance in the same way as W&W but field-normalizes performance; failure to control properly can inflate apparent gender/nepotism effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret success rates in context (scheme-specific comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare gendered success rates within the specific grant scheme or panel rather than using broader-council aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors highlight that overall council-level success-rate differences (e.g., 5–10%) are not the same as the specific scheme under study (where male success was 26% vs female 8% in the focal year); small sample counts in a scheme can make percentage differences large and volatile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data provenance, correction and replication sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent about dataset versions and corrections because reanalyses can reach different conclusions depending on data cleaning and corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note other reanalyses (Sandström & Riis) obtain different conclusions after dataset corrections; replication requires sharing datasets or documenting corrections and analytical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple indicators and approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate bias assessment using different indicators, models and robustness checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper expands original analyses by using field-normalization, panel-standardization, GLMs, and alternative regressions; using multiple methods showed reduced effect sizes compared to the original claim and highlighted sensitivity to analytical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and share supplementary materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide supplementary files and documentation of methods, data processing, and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes a supplementary DOCX and references data provenance (dataset provided by Sandström); sharing supplementary materials aids reproducibility and critique.
